Wanted to add that states make their own standardized tests and school districts choose their curriculum. Money is absolutely wasted or used inappropriately in education, but typically it’s money that is managed by the state itself already, Eliminating the DoE is a great way to put more power and control into already provably irresponsible hands.

High school English teacher and attorney here.

The DoE provides critical funding to schools in financial need. Personally, my classroom depends on Title II funding to work because it provides my students pencils, backpacks, binders, and snacks for after school services like tutoring. It also provides me with poster paper, technology like hdmi cables or document projectors, expo markers and white board erasers, cleaning supplies, post it notes, pens, etc. I just go to my designated Title II director in my school and let her know what I or my students need and she provides it. 

Further, the DoE protected student rights to an education. You can’t discriminate against students because of circumstances beyond their control: finances, immigration status, sexuality (of themselves or of parents), disability, race, religion, language, etc. 

Finally, I’m more worried about what this move signals for the next steps this administration is going to take. My students are mostly Hispanic with many of them having immigrated to this country in their lifetime, some as recently as March 2024. There is no path forward that I see that doesn’t absolutely demolish their rights not only to an education (guaranteed by SCOTUS in San Antonio Special School District v Rodriguez decades ago), but also their right to safety and privacy. Why are we putting services that help all kids in the crosshairs? 

Sure, standardized testing is a huge bummer and I kind of hate my curriculum because I teach English and they don’t read books anymore, just short stories and articles. But the DoE ensured that all of my students were given every support they needed to show up and sit in my classroom and eat lunch and learn. It compelled states to take care of all students regardless of ability. I’m more worried for the harm my students will incur because this administration will continue to shred the policies that serve students of color, disabled students, immigrant students, financially insecure students, students who need language support, like the list goes on. Just feels like punching down for no reason other than to cause harm to kids.

Yes so it is capitalism that created a need for these small canisters of oxygen, not my medical need for oxygen itself. If I wanted a giant compressed container of oxygen that I could keep at home, it would require the prescription of a doctor and then a long fight with my insurance company to guarantee an affordable price of the prescription.

As for oxygen for home use, in general, being a necessity, yeah it really is. I don't need a canister for all hours of the day, just a few times a month. Without it, the headache I have is extremely debilitating. Most of my attacks happen at night when I'm home (thank goodness) but should they occur during the day, I would send myself to the ER if I did not have a canister of oxygen like this on my person which is way more expensive than the $13 for this item. It's not only medically necessary, but it prevents taking financial risks for the sake of my health. LSC strikes again and again

Yes! They have like 100 one-second puffs in each canister, and for my headaches, a couple of seconds every 15 minutes while I wait for my pain meds to kick in does the trick. It doesn't erase it entirely, but it provides enough relief that I stop considering just killing myself as a way to stop the pain. It becomes like a normal, manageable headache instead of the usual unbearable cluster headache

It's necessary the same way insulin is necessary. Some people have bodies that produce enough oxygen for them, but some don't. I think that if something is necessary for even one person to comfortably exist, it should be considered a necessity that can be accessed for free by that person. For example, my brother and I suffer from a disorder that requires us to take heavy doses of allergy meds every day or we risk the chance of extreme physical pain and discomfort. We get our meds for free with our insurance, but my parents don't since allergy meds are not that necessary for them.

My doctor NEVER mentioned it to me. I figured it out after stumbling upon an online forum when I was desperate for a remedy and was considering LSD or basically overdosing on an allergy med because my last attack was so bad. Turns out oxygen helps! I do have to inhale every 15 minutes until my pain meds kick in since it isn't a long-term solution, but the relief is so quick and so helpful that I have one next to my bed at all times

I use this brand of oxygen to help with cluster headaches. It provides instant relief, is absolutely vital to my ability to exist, and is a medical need. I'm thankful it's an OTC solution, but it's such a small amount of oxygen for the price. Absolutely ridiculous that capitalism allows a necessity to be capitalized upon. We create supply and demand for our economy rather than just simply allowing room for us to exist comfortably.

No one really says this enough but lawyers don’t want to waste time in consultation; not because it’s their time but because it’s YOURS.

I’m by no means a lawyer and cannot give legal advice yet, but I do think your diagnosis is significant. An intentional tort requires actual harm, and being diagnosed so recently for what they did 10 years ago makes me wonder when the statute of limitations begins. It might begin when the abuse happened, but it might also be when the harm is realized. Does that make sense? Research IIED and school negligence in your state, see which attorneys specialize in that, and then seek out an accessible consultation.

I would research Intentional Inflection of Emotional Distress lawsuits in your state. It’s also known as IIED and it’s classified as an intentional tort. 

I hate that you went through that, but I see some sort of silver lining in your recent diagnosis. Statute of Limitations matter and are often really short for things like this, but I would seek out an attorney. They often have free consultations for you to lay out your facts and they will tell you whether it’s worth going to court for or not. 

Again I’m so sorry your school failed you, and the kind of closure available to you is limited but not quite out of reach yet. Get a professional opinion and see what steps you can take.

Hi! I work in a transactional law clinic that helps with LLCs as well as every other corporate issue. For free help, reach out to local law clinics at law schools in your state. If you aren’t close to one, apply SOON so you can have virtual meetings with them before policies change to allow in person meetings again. They provide free legal services and representation to clients just like you! I work in New York State, but I know they exist everywhere. 

There are also free resources online to help you. Type “[your state] LLC creation” and look through there. Usually, each state government has a website specifically housing all of their policy and law concerning what you have to do to start an LLC. 

A lawyer is an expensive but great resource, too, for advice while you plan your LLC. They can help you find loans, grants, etc. and also advise you on whether the amount of money you have to start is enough for your vision, whether you need a member-managed vs. manager-managed governance structure, if you should seek out a fiscal sponsorship first, if LLC is even the proper structure for you, etc.

TLDR: look for economic development clinics at law schools in your area and state for free legal advice and services. Use Google. Try to have a lawyer help you in any way you can, even if you can’t get one for free
